summary: Describes server pool policies for Reliable Server Pooling, including how to implement them at ENRP servers and for pool users. Policies decide which member of a pool should be chosen when a client asks for a server. It is published as an experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: When several cashiers are free, how do you decide who serves the next customer? This lists the rules, such as taking turns or picking the least busy.

questions: server selection policy round robin least used
subtitle: Server selection policies for Reliable Server Pooling.

tldr.problem: When a client needs a server from a pool of identical or similar servers, which one should it choose? Different applications need different strategies: some need simplicity, others need to avoid overloading busy servers.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines nine server selection policies: five non-adaptive (round-robin, weighted round-robin, random, weighted random, priority) and four adaptive (least-used, least-used with degradation, priority least-used, randomized least-used). Non-adaptive policies use static rules; adaptive policies use real-time load information.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can choose or combine policies based on their application's needs. The policies work with ENRP servers to make distributed load-balancing decisions.

today: RFC 5356 is an Experimental protocol defining policies for the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) architecture. RSerPool itself remains experimental. These policies are referenced by RFC 5354 and implemented in the control plane of ASAP and ENRP.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
The Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) protocols support multiple ways to select which server in a pool should handle a new request. This RFC describes the policies themselves and how both the ENRP server (which maintains pool state) and the pool user (client) should implement them.

The RFC defines two key terms: load (how much a server's resources are currently used, from 0 for idle to 0xffffffff for fully loaded) and weight (a server's relative capacity, where weight 100 is twice as capable as weight 50). Both are application-specific; the protocol does not define what they measure.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to pick a server from a group depend on what matters most: speed, fairness, efficiency, or spreading the work around.

sections.title: Non-Adaptive Policies
sections.content:
Round Robin (RR) is the simplest: maintain a circular list of servers and hand out each new request to the next server in turn. This is the default policy and all RSerPool implementations must support it.

Weighted Round Robin (WRR) adds weights: servers with higher weight appear more often in the list, so they handle proportionally more requests.

Random picks a server at random each time, with no memory of previous choices. Weighted Random does the same but favors higher-weight servers.

Priority always selects the highest-priority server available, regardless of load. These five policies are non-adaptive: they do not change based on whether a server is busy.
sections.plainLanguage: Round-robin takes turns fairly. Weighted round-robin takes turns but lets strong servers take more turns. Random picks a name out of a hat. Priority always picks the boss if available.

sections.title: Adaptive Policies
sections.content:
Least Used (LU) asks each server how busy it is and routes new requests to the least-busy one. The ENRP server returns candidates sorted by load, lowest first.

Least Used with Degradation (LUD) goes further: it estimates that accepting a new request will increase a server's load and accounts for this. An ENRP server tracks how many clients have already been sent to each server and factors in that increase when calculating the best choice.

Priority Least Used (PLU) combines priority levels with load awareness: servers report both their current load and their load degradation value, and the ENRP server selects based on the lowest sum.

Randomized Least Used (RLU) blends randomness with load: the probability of selecting a server is proportional to how much of its capacity is still free (0xffffffff minus its load). These four policies are adaptive: they respond to real-time server state.
sections.plainLanguage: Adaptive policies watch how busy each server is and try to keep all of them equally busy. Some predict how much busier they'll get, and some still add a random element.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
For non-adaptive policies, the ENRP server maintains the list of pool members and the pool user (client) applies the policy to the list returned. For example, in Round Robin, ENRP holds a circular list and advances a pointer each time, ensuring different clients get different starting points.

For adaptive policies, ENRP does more work: it must select the best candidates based on load values received from each server and return them sorted. ENRP servers MUST NOT list the same server twice, and they SHOULD return enough candidates to give clients good backup options.

Clients SHOULD request multiple entries for adaptive policies and try them in order until one succeeds. ENRP servers MAY implement these policies differently than specified, as long as the results are compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: The ENRP server either maintains a fair list (for simple policies) or picks the best servers (for smart ones). Clients use the list either by going in order or by picking randomly.

sections.title: Policy Parameter Format and Registry
sections.content:
Each policy is encoded as a 32-bit Policy Type value. The format uses two flag bits plus a 30-bit policy number: the X bit marks user-defined policies; the A bit marks adaptive policies. For example, Round Robin is 0x00000001 (not adaptive, non-user-defined, number 1). Least Used is 0x40000001 (adaptive, number 1).

Nine policy types are registered: Round Robin (0x00000001) through Priority (0x00000005) for non-adaptive, and Least Used (0x40000001) through Randomized Least Used (0x40000004) for adaptive. The range 0x80000000 to 0xffffffff is reserved for private, non-standard policies. Any new policies must be registered with IANA using the Specification Required process.
sections.plainLanguage: Each policy gets a unique number. The first bit says whether it's adaptive. You can invent your own policies using a private range.

items.title: Round Robin
items.text: Take turns fairly; MUST be supported by all implementations.

items.title: Weighted Round Robin
items.text: Take turns, but strong servers take more.

items.title: Random
items.text: Pick any server randomly each time.

items.title: Priority
items.text: Always pick the highest-priority available server.

items.title: Least Used
items.text: Route to the least-busy server right now.

items.title: Least Used with Degradation
items.text: Predict how busy it will get and pick accordingly.

items.title: Priority Least Used
items.text: Consider priority plus load plus degradation.

items.title: Randomized Least Used
items.text: Pick randomly but favor less-busy servers.
